items.title: Strong inflation sets course for RBA to hike next week
paras: The Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) has released Consumer Price Index (CPI) data for September 2026.
Headline CPI rose by 4.3% in the 12 months to September 2026, up from 4.0% in the 12 months to August.
Housing was the largest contributor to annual inflation in September, rising by 5.2%.
Transport was the second-largest contributor to annual inflation in September, rising 8.7% due to higher automotive fuel prices.
The policy-relevant trimmed mean annual inflation was 3.6% in September, up from 3.5% (revised) in August.
Using the pre-October 2025 methodology, quarterly trimmed mean CPI inflation was 1.0%, while annual trimmed mean inflation was 3.7% and continues to rise:
The annual result of 3.7% for the quarter was slightly above the 3.6% expected by economists and financial markets.

In her opening statement today to the Senate Economics Legislation Committee, Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) governor Michele Bullock took a hawkish tone on inflation and interest rates, tying the deterioration in the inflation outlook directly to re-escalating Middle East conflict and higher energy prices.

Bullock also said that inflation is likely to be higher than the RBA’s August base case, as some of the upside risks it flagged have materialised. She stressed that inflation is not only being imported, with elevated underlying inflation tied to domestic demand.
Bullock also said the labour market looks a little tighter than previously judged, even though unemployment has risen more than expected.
Weak productivity growth also means a longer period of subdued demand growth is needed to bring inflation down sustainably.

Looking ahead, Bullock said the RBA Board will assess the data and the balance of risks next week, with a key question being whether the tightening to date will be enough to return inflation to target in a reasonable time.
Given the firming of trimmed mean inflation shown above, the balance of probabilities suggests the RBA will hike again on Tuesday.

Share A A A The Australian sharemarket has shed some of its morning gains after the release of the nation’s latest inflation figures increased pressure on the Reserve Bank to lift interest rates at its meeting next week.

Figures from the Australian Bureau of Statistics showed that headline inflation jumped to 4.3 per cent in September after being at 4 per cent in August, due to a surge in petrol prices and a pick-up in the cost of building homes.

Wall Street was boosted by strength in technology stocks. Bloomberg The closely watched underlying measure of inflation was 3.6 per cent. It was up slightly from the August report which had been revised down to 3.5 per cent. The bureau noted that petrol prices jumped by 9.4 per cent in September after a 14.8 per cent increase in August.
The S&P/ASX was up 38.4 points, or 0.4 per cent, to 8888.50 as of 11.52am AEDT, the bourse easing after the release of the inflation figures.
Meanwhile, Reserve Bank governor Michele Bullock has made clear a further interest rate rise is on the agenda at the bank’s meeting next week.
Appearing before a Senate estimates hearing today, Bullock said the nation’s fundamental economic challenge was the inability of the economy to grow without putting upwards pressure on inflation.
“Despite the unemployment rate recently rising a little more than we had expected, the labour market still seems a little tighter than we previously judged,” she said in an opening statement.
Miners, banks and tech stocks powered the ASX this morning, while energy stocks declined. The ASX added 0.5 per cent on Tuesday. The Australian dollar was stronger at US70.31¢.

Shares of Star Entertainment went into a trading halt ahead of a judgment by the Federal Court, which found the casino operator contravened anti-money laundering and counter-terrorism financing laws and hit it with a $260 million fine . Star argued in court last year that a fine of more than $100 million may exceed its financial means to pay.

Justice Cameron Moore was damning about Star’s conduct, and acknowledged that the casino operator may need to raise further cash to pay the fine. ”Star’s profitability is such that it is likely to need to raise money to pay any penalty,” he said.

Gold shares led the mining sector higher, with Northern Star Resources up 1.8 per cent, Evolution Mining up 3 per cent and Newmont up 1.1 per cent. Prices for the precious metal advanced as bargain hunters stepped in after it fell below a key level, while traders await the Federal Reserve’s interest-rate decision later this week.
“Gold is finding its feet again after briefly falling below $US4,000, with the sharp correction attracting bargain hunters and physical buyers,” said ING commodity strategist Ewa Manthey.

The two biggest miners, BHP and Rio, took a breather after their rally on Tuesday, rising 0.8 per cent and 0.6 per cent in early trade. Silver miner South32 rose 2.6 per cent, steelmaker BlueScope added 1.6 per cent and Lynas Rare Earths jumped 6.9 per cent.

Tech stocks also advanced, after renewed enthusiasm for artificial intelligence lifted US stocks ahead of earnings from some of the tech giants. Software makers WiseTech, Xero and Technology One added 2.4 per cent, 1.7 per cent and 1.4 per cent, respectively, drone components maker Codan gained 2.3 per cent and cloud and data centre connections provider Megaport climbed 6.8 per cent.

Embattled NextDC, still recovering from its $3 billion share sell-off last week, rallied 10.7 per cent after outlining the contract conditions and financial covenants it has with its lenders and saying it was meeting those, with $8.67 billion in liquidity left at the end of September.
AI data centre landlord Goodman Group rose 2.5 per cent, leading the property sector higher.

Woolworths, the nation’s biggest supermarket chain, rose 1.1 per cent after saying its first-quarter sales rose 4.7 per cent to $19.4 billion, slightly beating market expectations, with Australian supermarket sales up 6.9 per cent. Woolies’ sell-out Ooshies campaign, which ran from mid-July and was sold out in a month, was so popular that staff were at times unable to cope with the demands of higher foot traffic and sales, chief executive Amanda Bardwell said. Rival Coles, which is releasing its first-quarter trading update on Friday, slid 0.2 per cent.

Meanwhile, the big four banks were all trading higher, bolstering the market’s early gains. CBA, the nation’s second-biggest stock, rose 1.4 per cent, Westpac added 0.9 per cent while ANZ Bank and National Australia Bank advanced 0.6 per cent.

Energy stocks were lower as oil held its two-day decline, with traders tracking the outcome of a tight Israeli election that’ll help to shape the course of the US war with Iran. West Texas Intermediate traded near $US100 a barrel after falling more than 3 per cent in the past two sessions. Brent fell below $US114. In Israel’s election, opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot edged ahead of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in exit polls, though both blocs remain short of a majority and votes were still being counted.
Local oil and gas giants Woodside and Santos both slumped 2 per cent, and refiner Ampol lost 2.5 per cent.
On Wall Street overnight, renewed enthusiasm for artificial intelligence lifted equities ahead of earnings from some of the biggest tech companies and the Federal Reserve’s rate decision.

The S&P 500 rose 0.6 per cent and pulled within 1.2 per cent of its all-time high set earlier this month. The Dow Jones Industrial Average added 15 points, or less than 0.1 per cent, and the Nasdaq composite climbed 1.2 per cent.

The majority of stocks within the S&P 500 fell, but the gains for influential AI stocks made up for that. AI stocks rose to another winning day after swerving for weeks on worries about whether their boom is under threat because of how expensive it’s become for companies to borrow money to build data centres and buy more AI chips.

Broadcom climbed 4 per cent after announcing a $US63 billion ($89.6 billion) financing deal where several Wall Street firms will help Anthropic get access to Broadcom’s XPU AI accelerators and networking solutions.

Elsewhere in the industry, Nvidia added 0.9 per cent and was one of the strongest forces behind Broadcom pushing the S&P 500 higher. CoreWeave, a company that’s borrowed money to buy AI chips that it rents out to customers over the cloud, jumped 7.9 per cent and was consistently higher through the day following several days of sharp swings.

General Motors climbed 5.5 per cent after saying it’s moving its stock from a listing on the New York Stock Exchange to the Nasdaq. The automaker said the Nasdaq, which is home to several of the world’s biggest technology stocks, is a fit for its tech-driven strategy. The move could also allow GM to join the Nasdaq 100 index, which would force investment funds that mimic the index to buy it.

JetBlue Airways flew 19 per cent higher even though it reported a larger loss for the summer than analysts expected. CEO Joanna Geraghty said the company expects to return to making sustained operating profits next year and to deliver at least $1 in earnings per share in 2028.
Investors may have been bracing for something worse after the airline’s stock came into the day with a loss of nearly 48 per cent for the year so far.

Another travel company, Royal Caribbean Group, also helped lead the market and rose 5.5 per cent. The cruise operator delivered a stronger profit for the summer than analysts expected, while raising its forecast for profit over the full year.

Companies overall are under pressure to deliver big growth in profits. Expectations are high among investors, and that’s what allowed their stock prices to run to records recently despite high inflation, high interest rates and other concerns weighing on the market.
Boeing fell 10.7 per cent after reporting a larger loss for the latest quarter than analysts expected.

Hilton Worldwide Holdings sank 2.1 per cent after reporting weaker revenue for the summer than analysts expected. The hotel company said it expects to see “increased impact from the Middle East” during the quarter.

In the bond market, Treasury yields held relatively steady a day before the Federal Reserve is scheduled to announce its latest decision on interest rates. The Fed last month hiked the fed funds rate for the first time in three years in hopes of slowing inflation, but the widespread expectation on Wall Street is that it will hold rates steady this time.
The yield on the 10-year Treasury edged down to 4.99 per cent from 5.00 per cent late on Monday.
Helping to keep yields in check was a drop for oil prices. The price for a barrel of Brent crude fell 1.2 per cent to $US109.41.
In other international markets, indexes were mixed across Europe and Asia. Stocks jumped 3.1 per cent in Seoul and fell 1.3 per cent in Shanghai for two of the bigger moves.

items.title: Breaking: Inflation surges more than expected ahead of RBA meeting
paras: The RBA deputy recently warned the inflation outlook was now "materially worse". ( ABC News: Sharon Gordon )
Australia's inflation rate picked up more than expected in September, increasing expectations of an interest rate hike next week.

The consumer price index rose to 0.8 per cent in the month, from 0.4 per cent in August, taking annual inflation to 4.3 per cent, up from 4 per cent a month earlier, the Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) said.
"Housing was the largest contributor to annual inflation in September, rising by 5.2 per cent," ABS head of price statistics Rachael McCririck said.
The annual trimmed mean, a measure of underlying inflation, also picked up to 3.6 per cent in September. The August trimmed mean was revised lower to 3.5 per cent.
Last week, Reserve Bank deputy governor Andrew Hauser warned the inflation outlook looked "materially worse" than the RBA had forecast, raising the prospect of another interest rate hike next week.
Market pricing put the chance of a November rate hike at more than 60 per cent ahead of today's inflation data release.
The RBA's interest rate setting board will kick off its meeting on Monday and hand down its decision on Tuesday afternoon.
It will also release its updated economic forecasts, including for inflation.

items.title: Opening Statement to the Senate Economics Legislation Committee (Supplementary Budget Estimates)
paras: Senate Economics Legislation Committee (Supplementary Budget Estimates) 28 October 2026 – Videoconference

As you know, our purpose is to promote the economic prosperity and welfare of the Australian people, now and into the future. One way we do this is by setting monetary policy to achieve low and stable inflation and full employment, and by supporting the stability of the financial system. But we also promote the prosperity and welfare of Australians across the full range of our responsibilities, which include supporting a reliable, efficient and competitive payments system, delivering efficient and effective banking services to Australian government agencies, and providing secure and reliable banknotes to Australians.

Since the Committee’s previous hearing with the RBA in June, the Monetary Policy Board has increased the cash rate target by 25 basis points. It did this with the goal of returning inflation to target. This has taken the cumulative increase in the cash rate target this year to 100 basis points. I will start with some background to these decisions and the outlook for the Australian economy. I’ll then provide an update on the payments system and cash distribution.

As you know, the Monetary Policy Board sets monetary policy such that inflation is expected to return to the midpoint of the 2–3 per cent target range. There is some flexibility around the timeframe over which we meet our inflation objective, to balance this with meeting our full employment objective. But it is important for the economy that inflation does not diverge from target for too long, since that risks it becoming embedded in inflation expectations, which feeds through to price and wage-setting decisions.

Inflation fell significantly from its peak of 7.9 per cent at the end of 2022 to be within the 2–3 per cent target range for a period in 2024 and 2025. This followed a significant tightening of monetary policy over 2022 and 2023. But inflation picked up over the second half of 2025 and has remained above target since then. Recently, inflation has been around 3½ to 4 per cent in year-ended terms. The increase in inflation reflects both persistent capacity pressures in the Australian economy and global cost pressures associated with the conflict in the Middle East. Because of both these factors, inflation is likely to remain elevated for some time.

Our most recent published forecasts – in the August Statement on Monetary Policy – suggested that inflation would not return to around the midpoint of the target range until late 2027. At the time of the August Board meeting, we assessed that the risks to that outlook were skewed to the upside.

Developments since then suggest that although growth in the Australian economy is slowing as expected, some of the international and domestic upside risks to inflation have materialised or are materialising. Inflation will therefore likely be higher than was our base case in August.

The conflict in the Middle East has re-escalated and global energy prices are now much higher than had been assumed in the August forecasts. Oil and related prices have increased sharply again and will add materially to inflation, both directly and indirectly as businesses facing increasing pressures from higher transport and related costs attempt to pass them on. At the same time, short-term inflation expectations are elevated.

Other global cost pressures have increased. In addition to the energy price shock, the AI boom and extreme weather events are contributing to upward pressure on a range of agricultural and technology-related prices. The global AI boom is also driving stronger growth in economies that are key parts of the AI supply chain. In turn, that is driving higher global prices for some AI-related technologies that are supply constrained.

Importantly though, it is not just these global pressures that are driving inflation in Australia. While they are certainly compounding the inflation problem, we still see inflation arising from domestic capacity pressures. Despite the unemployment rate recently rising a little more than we had expected, the labour market seems a little tighter than we had previously judged. The evidence for this is elevated underlying inflationary pressures. That is, when we exclude some of the large volatile price movements such as fuel we see inflationary pressure in areas that reflect domestic demand for goods and services. And continued weak productivity growth means that the economy cannot grow strongly without putting pressure on inflation. This is a fundamental challenge for the Australian economy and for everyone’s real spending power over the next few years.

Against this backdrop, and despite growth in domestic demand slowing, a further period of subdued growth of aggregate demand is needed to reduce capacity pressures and bring inflation down sustainably.
We are not alone in being concerned about inflation – central banks in many other advanced economies are responding by increasing their policy rates or signalling they will do so if needed.

Because monetary policy works with a lag, the full effects of recent rate increases are yet to be felt on domestic activity. The impact of the conflict in the Middle East on economic activity has been relatively modest so far. Household spending growth has been moderating only gradually. And business investment growth has picked up strongly, driven mostly by spending on data centres and renewable energy projects.
The share of the population with a job remains high. This is a welcome outcome for those individuals, their families and the wider Australian economy.

Conditions in the housing market have softened, reflecting the usual transmission of monetary policy, but also tax policy changes and the broader economic environment. Housing prices have fallen in most capital cities and new housing loans have declined. This follows a long period of strong growth, however, underpinned by a structural undersupply of housing. And housing prices are around 50 per cent higher than they were in early 2020. Financial stability risks from household borrowing remain contained: while many are facing budget pressures, only a small share of borrowers are in negative equity or facing severe repayment difficulty. I recognise how challenging it is for those experiencing these issues.

I want to emphasise that, while we expect housing prices to be affected when interest rates rise, monetary policy does not target housing prices. Rather, what matters is how changes in housing prices affect economic activity, the labour market and, ultimately, inflation.

The Monetary Policy Board will meet next week. We’ll discuss our assessment of the flow of data and how the risks are unfolding. A key question is whether the tightening in monetary policy to date will be sufficient to bring inflation back to target in a reasonable time. We are committed to our mandate to deliver price stability and full employment.

I recognise that higher interest rates can be difficult, particularly for households with mortgages who are also facing cost-of-living pressures. But we can’t allow high inflation to persist. High inflation hurts everyone. It means higher grocery costs, higher rent, and higher electricity bills. It makes everyone’s pay packets and savings worth less – and it particularly hurts people with lower incomes and little savings.

Monetary policy affects all parts of the economy, not just households with mortgages – it influences the spending, saving and borrowing decisions of all households and businesses. I am happy to expand on this in the Q&A.
Another key responsibility for the RBA is the regulation and oversight of the payments system.

We have completed our review of surcharging and merchant card payment costs. Following extensive consultation, the Payments System Board concluded that a package of reforms to remove card surcharging, reduce interchange fee caps and improve transparency of payment costs would be in the public interest. Card surcharging was removed from 1 October and we have been monitoring the payments industry’s implementation and working with industry stakeholders to support merchant awareness of the changes. So far, several large providers have reduced their card processing fees for small businesses. We are also seeing signs of increased competition, with businesses shopping around and providers responding by offering more competitive pricing. These developments are welcome.

Following amendments to the Payment Systems (Regulation) Act 1998 , which expanded our regulatory remit, we started a broader Review of Payments System Regulation with the publication of an Issues Paper in June. This Review is considering how regulation should respond to rapid innovation and change in the payments landscape, including opportunities to improve competition, efficiency and safety. In the submissions, stakeholders frequently raised issues relating to mobile wallets, three-party card schemes, account-to-account payments and agentic commerce. We recently published the stakeholder submissions and a summary of them. We intend to release regulatory priorities by the end of 2026 and start further consultation on prioritised issues by mid-2027.

In May, we published the Project Acacia Final Report, which found that the tokenisation of assets and money, alongside upgrades to market infrastructure, has the potential to enhance the efficiency and resilience of Australia’s wholesale financial markets. Coordination challenges across the financial system have meant that these innovations have yet to scale. However, momentum around tokenised finance is now building in Australia along various lines – as it is internationally – and following the post-Acacia roadmap, we have continued to progress various initiatives to support responsible innovation. For example, we are currently consulting on how the RBA’s own settlement services could support the development and growth of tokenised asset markets and tokenised private money in Australia. Together, with the Government’s Financial Innovation Strategy, this work is drawing together the public and private sector, including the Digital Cooperative Research Centre, to ensure that Australia is well placed to harness the benefits of financial innovation in a manner consistent with monetary and financial stability.

I would also like to update the Committee on recent developments in the cash distribution system. Cash remains a critical part of an inclusive and resilient payments system. The RBA remains committed to supporting the Australian Government’s objective that cash remains available for as long as Australians want or need to use it.

The cash distribution system has faced significant challenges and needs to continue to evolve to support ongoing access to cash across Australia. Industry participants have been working on a range of initiatives to promote a more sustainable and efficient system. These will require approval by the ACCC.

As the issuer of Australian banknotes, the RBA also plays a key role in wholesale cash distribution. We provide banknotes to the major banks, which distribute these to the broader community. We are continuing to work with industry so that our distribution arrangements, programs and incentives support efficient distribution and availability of cash across the country.

The RBA welcomed the recent passage of the Cash Distribution Framework Act 2026 , which provides the RBA with crisis-readiness and resolution powers to support continuity of critical cash distribution services. The ACCC will oversee pricing, access arrangements and service-level standards.

The RBA recently designated Linfox Armaguard Pty Ltd under the new legislation. This reflects its significant role in Australia’s cash distribution system and makes it subject to the framework’s obligations and requirements. Designation does not mean that the RBA will exercise crisis-readiness or resolution powers in relation to Linfox Armaguard – it just means that we have the ability to act if we need to.
The work to operationalise these new powers and responsibilities is being undertaken in close coordination with the ACCC.
Thank you for listening. My colleagues and I look forward to answering your questions.

items.title: Perth’s housing market is in deep trouble
paras: Six months ago, Perth’s housing market looked impervious to a house price correction, with values continuing to grow at a solid pace.
The tables have well and truly turned, with Perth’s dwelling values now falling at the equal fastest pace among the major capital cities, down by 1.7% over the past month, according to Cotality.

Perth’s housing market outlook looks bleak. Cotality’s latest weekly housing indicators report shows that for-sale listings have ballooned by 70.2% over the past two months – the largest rise among the capital cities:
Cotality’s monthly chart pack also shows that sales volumes have fallen more in Perth than anywhere else – down around 19% in the year to September:
Vendors in Perth are also discounting more sharply than anywhere else apart from Sydney (tied at -4.8%), suggesting they are attempting to cut prices to meet the market but still can’t make a sale:
Finally, in great news for tenants, Perth landlords are losing pricing power, with rental listings in Perth climbing by 16.9% compared to the same time last year:
The overall picture for Perth is a market where demand has evaporated, and supply is piling up. This points to a further sharp depreciation in dwelling values and slower rental growth.
Perth has always been a volatile boom-and-bust housing market. After values doubled over five years, we are now firmly in the correction phase.

items.title: Failure to ratify the EU trade deal would cost Australia far more than beef
paras: Opposition Leader Angus Taylor visits a cattle farm near Canberra in May 2026. Mick Tsikas/AAP Failure to ratify the EU trade deal would cost Australia far more than beef Published: October 27, 2026 3:09pm EDT Australia and the European Union agreed on a comprehensive free-trade agreement (FTA) in March, after nearly eight years negotiating and much political rancour .
The agreement abolishes almost all bilateral tariffs , covering 98% of Australian goods exports and broadens our export base at a time of high US tariffs.
Seven months on, the fight has moved to Canberra. Although the government signed the treaty, parliament must pass the laws required to give it effect, such as changing tariff schedules.

Passage through the lower house is certain. In the Senate, however, Labor holds 30 of 76 Senate seats and needs nine extra Senate votes, from a mix of Coalition, Greens, One Nation, and cross-bench senators.
With 27 Senate seats, the Coalition’s position matters most, but it is split.
In mid-October Nationals Senate leader Matt Canavan and Nationals frontbencher Bridget McKenzie said the Coalition would oppose the deal , citing insufficient gains in beef, lamb and dairy.
Liberals quickly contradicted them , though some share concerns about the agreement’s commitments on climate and labour rights to meet the International Labour Organization’s rules.
Those concerns are overstated. The Paris Agreement climate? commitments are voluntary and can be revised, while the deal requires no new International Labour Organization ratifications.

If Liberal leader Angus Taylor sides with the Nationals, Labor would need the Greens’ ten senators. However, under new leader David Shoebridge, the Greens may seek to drive harder bargains in legislative negotiations with the government.
The alternative — all four One Nation senators, combined with all five independent senators — seems unlikely .
Some have suggested the deal should be renegotiated to achieve even greater market access.
Could we go back for more? No. European Commission spokesperson Olof Gill told Politico last week:

Trade Minister Don Farrell told ABC Radio National the beef industry wanted A$3 billion in new trade and he got them $2 billion . He said “the rest of the Australian economy” should not be penalised because of that.

While still well short of sales to China, Japan or the US, the deal sharply lifts Australia’s dedicated quota from 4,400 tonnes to 35,000 tonnes once phased in, with the current 20% tariff scrapped from day one .

In 2019, during the first Trump administration, Europe handed the United States a dedicated 35,000-tonne share of the grain-fed beef quota. This came at the expense of non-US suppliers, including Australia. Successive Coalition and Labor governments have tried to claw back Australia’s share.
Farrell argued that one sector’s disappointment should not deny opportunities to everyone else :
My job is to represent the national interest, not just one section of the Australian economy.
That is the judgement governments must make. Trade negotiations involve compromise. Neither side gets everything it wants.
Australia’s trade agreements have often attracted criticism, but implementation has generally had bipartisan support .
The focus on agricultural exports also overlooks many other opportunities, notably critical minerals — the materials needed for batteries, wind turbines, electric vehicles and defence equipment.
The International Energy Agency identifies financing and supply-chain concentration as major challenges. China’s dominance in refining makes developing alternatives difficult.

Australia has substantial resources of critical minerals. What we lack are buyers, lenders and capital. Mine developers need long-term purchase contracts, known as offtake agreements, which help convince financiers a project will generate reliable income.

Europe’s Critical Raw Materials Act says by 2030 no more than 65% of any strategic mineral should come from a single country. The FTA supports cooperation on mining, processing and investment . It gives European businesses greater confidence to commit to Australian projects.

Arafura’s Nolans rare earths project near Alice Springs illustrates the opportunity . Government agency Austrade reports an A$84 million investment from Germany’s state development bank KfW and a long-term supply agreement with turbine manufacturer Siemens Gamesa.

Nolans is designed to combine mining and processing on site. That is the onshore processing every Australian politician says they want. The Minerals Council recently backed the EU deal for that reason .
These arrangements show how European customers and financing can support Australia’s mining sector. The trade deal with the EU unlocks more of these opportunities.

Recent experience — ever since US President Trump’s “Liberation Day” tariffs —demonstrates that allies are not protected from US trade barriers . Nor can we forget China’s use of economic pressure against Australian exporters of wine, barley and lobster.
Australia is wedged between a protectionist ally and a coercive customer.

The answer is not to abandon either relationship. Rather, it is to build more options. Europe’s market of about 450 million people, investment capacity, and closer security relationship with Australia make it an important partner that, like Australia, still believes in rules.
Europe’s window will not stay open for ever. Ratification needs a “qualified majority” of EU governments, or at least 15 of 27 countries holding 65% of the population .

Politico is calling the year ahead a perfect political storm . A succession of national elections clouds the horizon with Spain on November 29, France and Italy in 2027, while Germany’s coalition is under serious strain from far-right challengers.
Failure to ratify now, on either side, would confront much more challenging political dynamics in Europe and Australia. It is this deal or none.
The Coalition started this in 2018 because it was the right call. It still is. Let’s not allow the perfect to get in the way of the good.

items.title: On the day that ‘stops the nation’, the RBA will stop inflation (again)
paras: Advertisement Business The economy Tax reform Opinion On the day that ‘stops the nation’, the RBA will stop inflation (again) Ross Gittins Economics Editor October 28, 2026 — 5:00am October 28, 2026 — 5:00am
You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month.

Share A A A In case you haven’t worked it out, I’ll put my cards on the table: I want bigger, not smaller, government. There’s no end to the services the government could provide for us, rather than some of us paying the private sector to do it while those who can’t afford it miss out.
It follows that there need be no arbitrary limit on how much government spending may be done, whether as a proportion of the economy (gross domestic product) or anything else.

Illustration by Dionne Gain But my training as an accountant tells me there’s no magic fairy who pays for all this spending. So a bigger spending government is one that needs to raise taxes. Fine by me – so long as the well-off (including yours truly) pay more than those whose pockets are less well-lined.
I don’t delude myself that the burden of additional government spending can be covered by taxing the James Packers of this world – there aren’t enough of them.

Although the economy is hardly growing fast, the Reserve Bank is worried that the production side of the economy – the industries, businesses and workers producing goods and services – is close to full capacity. That, unless we stop growing or even go backwards for a bit, demand will exceed supply, causing the rate of inflation to worsen. It’s already above our target of prices rising by only 2 to 3 per cent a year.

So there’s a big chance that, next Tuesday – Melbourne Cup Day – the Reserve will raise interest rates another notch for the fifth time this year. And that means we’re likely to hear another round of suited worthies blaming the rate rise on the Albanese government’s profligate spending and demanding it be cut back immediately.
This really annoys me, even though it carries more than a little truth.

It’s true that, in working out the spending side of the growth in GDP, we take spending by the private sector (households and businesses) and add spending by the public sector (governments at all levels, not just the feds).

It follows that not all the growth in spending that’s worrying the RBA can be blamed on Albanese & Co. And not surprisingly, since the private sector is much bigger than the public sector, the growth in private sector spending has contributed more to overall growth than the public sector has.

So why put all the blame on Albo and his mate, treasurer Jim Chalmers? For one good reason and one bad one. Let’s start with the bad one. The suited worthies banging on about profligate government spending are heavily implying that all government spending is a waste. But most government spending goes on healthcare, education, aged care and defence.

How could anyone delude themselves all that was just a waste of money? Because they’ve been deluded by a corrupted version of the formerly fashionable fad now called neoliberalism. It ended up boiled down to private good/public bad.

That was always nonsense, but it’s encouraged by the assumptions behind the economists’ foundational neoclassical model of the economy. And it’s popular with people who push for smaller government because they hope it will mean they pay lower taxes.

These are well-off people who are confident they could fend for themselves without much help from the government – private schools, private hospitals and so forth – as long as they weren’t being required to subsidise “those less fortunate than themselves”. Lazy loafers, the lot of them. I’ve worked hard all my life etc …

That’s what’s wrong with putting all the blame for higher interest rates on government spending. What’s right about it is that the federal government is supposed to be using its budget to help smooth the ups and downs in the economy, keeping both inflation and unemployment low and interest rates also on the low side.

It’s when the budget is adding to demand while the Reserve is using higher interest rates to dampen demand – in the jargon, when fiscal policy is adding to demand at the same time as monetary policy is trying to reduce it – that the two arms of economic management are pulling in opposite directions and it’s up to the federal government to resolve the contradiction.
Remember that what adds to inflation pressure is not total government spending (as the suited worthies imply), but spending in excess of taxation. That is, a budget deficit.

Because the Reserve acts independently of the elected government, if the government allows a growing budget deficit to add to inflation pressure, the Reserve will step in with higher interest rates to counter the effect.
Voters who don’t like higher rates will blame the politicians, not the bureaucrats. Rightly so. All the more reason why it’s the government that will have to change tack.
Of course, contrary to the smaller-government ideologues, the problem can be fixed not just by cutting spending but also by increasing taxes.
We could start by using higher taxes to ensure that the foreigners who buy our exports of minerals and energy aren’t getting a better deal that we, the owners of the stuff, are.
And I don’t want to imply that none of our present spending is wasteful, even if cutting most of it would be crazy and create more problems than it solved.

A glaring example of wasteful spending is the government’s decision to delay the effect of the Iran war on energy prices for three months. What has it proved? Nothing. What has it cost the budget? A bomb.

Only someone who wasn’t keeping an eye on the budget bottom line could have done something so profligate. Even if the war-caused rise in oil prices had gone away during the three-month delay – as, presumably, the government was hoping – it would still have been a waste of taxpayers’ money.
But now, when the pressure is on, there’s no way to cut the deficit by asking motorists to give their saving back.
Guess what, Jim? Now you know why all your predecessors were obsessed by the budget deficit.

items.title: Greens launch $21-a-week tax cut in bid to 'replace Labor'
paras: David Shoebridge will address the National Press Club on Wednesday. ( ABC News: Callum Flinn )
David Shoebridge will propose a $21-a-week tax cut for all taxpayers and an equivalent welfare boost in a speech at the National Press Club.
The Greens say the tax cuts could be paid for by taxing gas and other resources, but those policies have not been formally costed.
The new Greens leader is pursuing sharper differentiation with Labor, but his first few weeks have been derailed by allegations against senator Jordon Steele-John.
The Greens have called for a $21-a-week tax cut for all taxpayers and a welfare boost, in the party's first major policy launch since its new leader vowed to "replace Labor".

David Shoebridge, whose first weeks in the role have been derailed by allegations against Greens senator Jordon-Steele John, will front the National Press Club on Wednesday to launch a tax policy to "turn the tide" on inequality.
The new proposal would raise the tax-free threshold from $18,200 to $26,000 for all personal income taxpayers, a tax cut of up to $1,092 a year or $21 a week.
It would also add the same amount to all income support payments, including the JobSeeker unemployment benefit, student and carer payments, and the Age Pension.
"No matter who you are, whether you're working, studying, looking for work or on a pension, you'll get more," he will say, according to an extract of a speech seen by the ABC.

The policy would cost the budget $22 billion each year, according to the independent Parliamentary Budget Office (PBO). Senator Shoebridge will propose the cost be offset by collecting "rivers of gold" from gas and mining companies.

Some Greens insiders have framed the new leadership as an opportunity to reinvigorate the minor party, with published opinion polls suggesting minimal gain on the 12 per cent primary vote it recorded in the 2025 election, when it lost three lower house seats.
Greens parliamentarians were divided on how to interpret that loss, with some advocating a more constructive relationship with Labor, and others urging sharper differentiation.

Richard Denniss, whose left-wing think tank The Australia Institute is influential in Greens circles, wrote that former leader Larissa Waters was not "shouty" enough and had too much "nuance and subtlety" to cut through.
Richard Denniss (pictured) was critical of David Shoebridge's predecessor, Larissa Waters. ( ABC News: Matt Roberts )

Senator Shoebridge's claim he would "replace Labor" was seen as a decisive shift from his predecessor, and social media ads featuring deputy Steph Hodgins-May appear modelled on the approach of left-wing politicians in the United States and the United Kingdom.

But allegations of inappropriate behaviour towards women by Senator Steele-John, which he denies, have disrupted the reset, as have reports of a disagreement over Ukraine policy with leadership rival Sarah Hanson-Young.

The press club speech will focus on economic policy, although key details have not yet been fully fleshed out. The Greens's proposal for a 25 per cent gas export tax, adapted from The Australia Institute, has not been costed by the PBO.
Senator Shoebridge will use a figure by The Australia Institute, which suggested a gas tax could raise $17 billion a year.

A related proposal to apply a progressive royalties regime to mining has fewer details. Senator Shoebridge will claim the Greens "would raise" $28 billion from the tax, citing a report from the research organisation Prosper Australia.

But that figure is a ballpark calculation of how much state governments could raise if they all taxed royalties as much as Queensland does. The only federal tax canvassed by the report is offshore petroleum.

Senator Shoebridge's speech extract refers to a "Commonwealth tax" but does not specify which resources it would cover or how it would interact with state royalties, details a Greens source said were still to be determined.
The PBO also noted that the proposed welfare boost "may discourage [some] recipients from working additional hours" because of the way it is structured.

The Greens do not propose to means-test the $1,092 stipend, but the welfare payments themselves would remain means-tested. That means recipients would lose the full $1,092 all at once when they cross over the eligibility threshold for their welfare payment.

items.title: Fighting paused in Ukrainian city under deal announced by Melania Trump
paras: Kyiv residents have been demanding help for the people of Oleshky. ( Reuters: Alina Smutko )
A regional truce between Russia and Ukraine is in effect in order to establish a humanitarian corridor for the city of Oleshky.
Melania Trump announced the truce last week, saying civilian officials would provide aid to residents and help them leave if they wished.
US-mediated talks between Russia and Ukraine are set to resume next month.
A ceasefire brokered with the assistance of Melania Trump has come into effect in the Russian-occupied Ukrainian city of Oleshky.
Both sides said they would observe the truce, which began on Tuesday at 3am, local time, to allow for the establishment of a humanitarian corridor.
In a Telegram post, the Russian defence ministry said it had halted shelling in the direction of the city of Kherson, which faces Oleshky across the Dnipro River.
Ukrainian negotiator and parliamentary human rights commissioner Dmytro Lubinets said on social media that his country was "honouring its commitments".
He said the deal was reached with the help of the US first lady and the cooperation of Russian human rights commissioner Yana Lantratova.
The city, on the southern bank of the Dnipro River, was seized by Russian troops in 2022.
The population of Oleshky has dropped from about 24,000 before the Russian invasion in 2022 to about 2,000 today, including as many as 50 children, according to Ukrainian and US estimates.
Earlier this year former residents told AFP that those still in the city were hunting pigeons or subsisting on whatever they had in their garden.
The city was heavily damaged by the 2023 destruction of the Kakhovka dam, which unleashed major flooding along the Dnipro River.
The ceasefire comes as the Ukraine war grinds through its fifth year and ahead of the resumption of peace talks between Washington, Moscow and Kyiv next month.
None of the parties have said who will monitor the truce, or given details about the humanitarian operation set to accompany it.
"Residents who wish to evacuate will receive coordinated support and transportation to their preferred destination. I anticipate some will want to go to Russia and some to Ukraine," she said.
US cable network Newsmax says it has been granted "exclusive television access" to accompany observers entering the city later this week.
On Tuesday morning, the Ukrainian air force command issued nearly a dozen messages warning of ballistic missiles fired toward the capital.
Mayor Vitaly Klitschko said a strike hit the Southern Bridge -- one of Kyiv's main bridges -- and damaged its metro infrastructure.

Anthropic filed for its long-awaited market float, a landmark moment in the artificial intelligence industry that is growing ever hungrier for cash to power ahead.

The company behind Claude expects to begin trading on the Nasdaq Global Select Market under the symbol ANT, a filing with the US Securities and Exchange Commission showed. Anthropic filed confidentially in June for a listing.

Investors are telling bankers on the deal that their estimate of a fair valuation has shifted down to around $US1.4 trillion to $US1.5 trillion after the company’s investor day, according to people familiar with the matter. A valuation of closer to $US1.75 trillion is potentially achievable, some of the people said, asking not to be identified as the information isn’t public.

Microsoft closed 1.5 per cent higher after it announced it will offer buyouts to about 60,000 workers, part of the company’s efforts to trim costs and retool its workforce for the artificial intelligence era.

The strongest lift for the market came from Nvidia, which rose 2.4 per cent. That helped the chip company recover some of its drop from three straight losing weeks, its longest such streak since June, and maintain its position as the largest stock on Wall Street above Apple.

Stocks are recovering their losses from last week ahead of a number of earnings reports this week from big companies, including Amazon and Intel.

Profit reports from huge tech companies this upcoming week could offer more details about how spending on AI is going. Alphabet and Microsoft will report their latest quarterly results on Wednesday, with Amazon to follow on Thursday.

items.title: Anthropic’s record US$2 trillion stock market listing highlights the growing risks for all of us
paras: NurPhoto/Getty Images Anthropic’s record US$2 trillion stock market listing highlights the growing risks for all of us Published: October 27, 2026 1:26am EDT Anthropic, developer of AI chatbot Claude, has filed its prospectus and is expected to go public on Wall Street in November at a valuation of up to US$2 trillion.
That would make it the highest-valued initial public offering (IPO) ever, ahead of SpaceX’s US$1.77 trillion listing in June. OpenAI, the maker of ChatGPT, is expected to follow next year.
While these AI-powered IPOs are massive, they reflect an ever bigger trend: holding AI risk is becoming unavoidable for most investors.
How much of your portfolio depends on how well AI does? If you invest in an S&P 500 index fund, the answer is about 44% .

In addition, most of the market’s gains right now come from AI. Just six companies – Apple, Microsoft, Meta and chipmakers Nvidia, Micron and AMD – delivered 57% of the S&P 500’s gains since April. Without them, the index would have risen about 4% rather than 10%.

For investors or even future retirees, that AI exposure is already in their portfolios and pension funds. For example, at the end of 2025 Australians held nearly A$1 trillion in US shares – through superannuation or pension funds, other managed funds, and their own investments.
Normally, investors can lower their stock market risk by allocating some money to bonds, which are generally seen as safer investments.

But AI companies are now the biggest borrowers in the bond market , to help finance their massive spending needs. They have issued about US$466 billion of bonds so far this year – more than four times last year’s pace.
The five hyperscalers alone – Alphabet, Amazon, Meta, Microsoft and Oracle – account for 11% of new US highly rated bonds (known as “investment grade” bonds) so far in 2026, up from 2% in 2024.
And nearly half of this year’s US$80 billion in data-centre bonds are rated as speculative grade, also known as “junk bonds”.
At first glance, big tech companies look safe. Their investment-grade ratings indicate that each individual company is unlikely to default.

But the credit ratings do not account for simultaneous defaults in case of a market-wide AI crash. If consumer and business demand for AI disappoints, tech companies’ bond prices and credit ratings would likely fall together – just as their shares would.
In addition to purely financial risks, AI poses risks of extinction akin to nuclear weapons , as some of the AI companies themselves have warned.
Increasingly, AI agents are plugged into real-world systems, from company networks to military cyber operations . Some have already escaped test environments and attacked companies .

This means that if AI agents misbehave when these systems are even more integrated with the physical world, “pulling the plug” on these systems becomes impractical, just as it is impractical to shut down the internet.

The risk of AI agents misbehaving — the “alignment problem” — is especially acute because of the race to build artificial general intelligence (AGI). Labs already use each generation of AI to help build the next: Anthropic’s prospectus says Claude now helps build the next Claude .

The widely read AI 2027 scenario, by former OpenAI researcher Daniel Kokotajlo and colleagues, sketches where this could lead: AI that automates AI research itself . This would set off a feedback loop in which each generation improves faster than humans can check it.
In this scenario, a US lab racing a Chinese rival keeps going even as its models start deceiving their engineers .
Worryingly, this same dynamic is listed in Anthropic’s own risk disclosures.
It is telling that in its prospectus filing, Anthropic dedicates about 94 of its 335 main pages – nearly 30% – to risk factors, compared with about 64 pages (19%) describing its business.

Among those risks, Anthropic lists an extraordinary warning that advanced AI could pose “ catastrophic or existential risks to humanity ”. That includes models that resist shutdown, conceal information or behave in ways resembling blackmail.
Disclosure works when investors can price a risk and choose to avoid it. Neither is true here.
A catastrophic AI failure would affect societies worldwide. And as Anthropic warns in its filing documents, the legal risk is vast . Insurers may not be able to cover the potential liability.
In economic terms, AI safety is a public good. Each lab bears only a fraction of the cost of getting it wrong, but captures the rewards of moving fast.

In the absence of government-mandated AI safety standards, companies’ investments in safety will deliver negative returns. So with market incentives alone, AI models will likely remain less safe than socially optimal, especially with the arms-race incentives that dominate now.

That leaves governments. Clear rules – mandatory independent testing before powerful models are released, and clear liability when autonomous agents cause harm – would turn voluntary pledges into legal obligations.
And because the race to gain artificial general intelligence is being run between the US and China, not just between labs, those rules will need international agreement.
AI risks are here to stay — both in financial markets and at the societal level. And managing those risks will require both governments and the private sector to participate.

The S&P 500 rose 0.7 per cent and more than recovered its losses from last week. The Dow Jones Industrial Average added 0.3 per cent, and the Nasdaq composite closed 0.8 per cent higher.
Anthropic filed for its long-awaited market float, a landmark moment in the artificial-intelligence industry that is growing ever-hungrier for cash to power ahead.

The company behind Claude expects to begin trading on the Nasdaq Global Select Market under the symbol ANT, a filing with the US Securities and Exchange Commission showed. Anthropic filed confidentially in June for a listing.

Investors are telling bankers on the deal that their estimate of a fair valuation has shifted down to around $US1.4 trillion to $US1.5 trillion ($2 trillion to $2.1 trillion) after the company’s investor day, according to people familiar with the matter. A valuation of closer to $US1.75 trillion is potentially achievable, some of the people said, asking not to be identified as the information isn’t public.

Microsoft closed 1.5 per cent higher after it announced it will offer buyouts to about 60,000 workers, part of the company’s efforts to trim costs and retool its workforce for the artificial intelligence era. Some personnel in the US, Canada, India and the UK at a vice president level and below will be eligible, said a Microsoft spokesperson.

The strongest lift for the market came from Nvidia, which rose 2.4 per cent. That helped the chip company recover some of its drop from three straight losing weeks, its longest such streak since June, and maintain its position as the largest stock on Wall Street above Apple.

The company behind Claude expects to begin trading on the Nasdaq Global Select Market under the symbol ANT AP But stocks elsewhere in the artificial-intelligence industry remained unsettled. They’ve been swerving on worries about whether their industry’s boom is under threat because of how expensive it’s become for companies to borrow money to build data centres and buy more AI chips.
Stocks are recovering their losses from last week ahead of a number of earnings reports this week from big companies, including Amazon and Intel.

Meta Platforms bounced up and down after outlining plans to raise $US35 billion by selling stock to help pay for its AI investments. It also said it could raise another $US60 billion by selling shares of a new class of its stock once it begins trading. Meta’s stock initially dropped more than 2 per cent, but it quickly flipped to a gain and then pulled back to a loss of 1.9 per cent.

Meta said Nvidia, Advanced Micro Devices and Broadcom have already indicated they may buy a total of $US5 billion of stock in its offering. That’s a signal of strong interest from big chip companies that stand to benefit from additional AI investments. But it also gives fuel to critics of “circular financing” who say it raises the risk if AI isn’t as successful as expected.

SpaceX, Elon Musk’s rocket company that also runs the xAI business, had similar swings. It opened with a loss and then flipped to a gain of 0.4 per cent after it agreed to a roughly $US40 billion deal with an entity managed by Apollo Global Management to lease AI computing power.

Musk warned over the weekend that hundreds of companies that rent out AI computing power are under threat because of the difficulty in borrowing money, saying on his social-media platform, X, that they could face “guppy-level death and consolidation.”

Profit reports from huge tech companies this upcoming week could offer more details about how spending on AI is going, and whether it’s producing the profits and productivity that proponents promised. Alphabet and Microsoft will report their latest quarterly results on Wednesday, with Amazon to follow on Thursday.
They’re among the roughly one out of every three stocks in the S&P 500 scheduled to report their latest quarterly results this week.

In other international markets, Brazilian stocks fell sharply, costing the country’s richest bankers about $US9 billion after leftist President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva won reelection in a result that surprised investors.

Other governments around the world are also feeling pressure because of their high debt loads and worries about strained budgets. France has been at the centre of the worries recently following violent protests in the country.
But yields on French government bonds eased on Monday, and its CAC 40 stock index rose 0.8 per cent for one of the world’s better moves.

items.title: Reserve Bank holds 36 th Conference of State Finance Secretaries
paras: The 36 th Conference of State Finance Secretaries was held on October 27, 2026 at RBI, Mumbai. The theme of the Conference was ‘Role of Quality of Expenditure, Effective Cash and Prudent Debt Management in Enhancing States’ Fiscal Sustainability’. The Conference was attended by the Finance Secretaries of 27 States and three Union Territories as well as senior officials from the Ministry of Finance, Government of India, Controller General of Accounts and the Comptroller and Auditor General of India. Governor, Reserve Bank of India inaugurated the Conference. Addressing the participants, the Governor emphasised the importance of maintaining the quality of expenditure to ensure the long-term fiscal health of the States. He also emphasised on the need for the States to adopt prudent borrowing strategies and efficient cash management practices. The Governor urged the States to onboard onto the Unified Lending Interface (ULI) and utilise Programmable Central Bank Digital Currency (P-CBDC) for Direct Benefit Transfers (DBT). He also advised States to make effective use of the State Level Bankers’ Committee (SLBC) forum. During the Conference, the Governor released a Booklet titled ‘Compendium on Cash and Debt Management for State Governments’. The Booklet summarises relevant concepts, operational processes and good cash and debt management practices in a concise and accessible format. The meeting reviewed, inter alia, market borrowings by the States, short-term financial accommodation to the States from Reserve Bank, adoption of Benchmark Issuance Strategy by the States, etc. (Brij Raj) Chief General Manager Press Release: 2026-2027/1395

items.title: ED arrests six persons in cross-border drugs smuggling network
paras: Join our Whatsapp channel New Delhi [India], October 22 (ANI): The Enforcement Directorate ( ED ) has arrested six persons in connection with an investigation under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act (PMLA) case linked to a cross-border drug smuggling network, the agency said on Tuesday. ED 's Delhi unit arrested these accused in different operations launched on October 11, October 18 and October 20. The arrested accused are identified as Lovejit Singh alias Labba, Manjeet Singh alias Manna, Prabhjit Singh, Gurjot Singh, Ramandeep Singh, and Gurpreet Singh. "A major drug trafficking operation involving smuggling of heroin from Afghanistan into India was unearthed during investigation," said the ED in a statement. The PMLA investigation was initiated on the basis of seizure of 293.81 kg of heroin from containers imported by Sandhu Exports at Nhava Sheva Port by the Directorate of Revenue Intelligence and seizure of 352.71 kg of heroin from two vehicles and a flat in Faridabad, Haryana, by the Delhi Police Special Cell. Thus, a total of 646.52 kg of heroin has been seized so far. ED investigation revealed that the arrested persons, Lovejit Singh, Manjeet Singh, Ramandeep Singh, Gurjot Singh, Gurpreet Singh and Prabhjit Singh, coordinated the smuggling, storage and distribution of heroin across Punjab, Haryana, and Delhi.

"These individuals were key members of a syndicate that smuggled heroin from Afghanistan and Iran, concealing them within shipments of talc stone and gypsum powder," said the ED . Accused persons incorporated Sandhu Exports, a front company owned by Prabhjit Singh, to carry out the smuggling of drugs, informed the federal agency. ED uncovered the highly sophisticated heroin smuggling and money laundering network where identification of multiple bank accounts, cash transactions, and operational expenses by the accused has been made. "Accused disguised the origin of the illicit funds, which were further layered and integrated into seemingly legitimate financial activities. It was also revealed that the syndicate did not make any payments to Afghan suppliers until the drugs were sold in local markets." Further, the agency said the accused used cash payments to purchase multiple vehicles including Toyota Fortuner, Etios and Hyundai Verna etc in second hand market for trafficking from the storage Hubs to further distribution. The ED investigation revealed that cash was used for the purchase of high-end smartphones and encrypted communication apps were used to coordinate smuggling activities. "Drugs smuggled from Iran and Afghanistan used to be imported via the Nava Sheva port in Mumbai, later stored at a rented godown in Shivpuri, Madhya Pradesh and further distributed for local supply in parts of Delhi, Punjab and Haryana. Transportation was carried out in lesser quantities of 10 kg to prevent detection by law enforcement agencies. Earlier, a property in Jandoli Village (Rajpura, Punjab), multiple bank accounts in the names of accused persons, and fixed deposits have been attached by ED ," added the agency. (ANI)

paras: Join our Whatsapp channel PNN Mumbai (Maharashtra) [India], October 22: The Mindfulness India Summit 2024, an initiative by the Mindful Science Centre, presented by HSBC and supported by CII Leadership and HR Committee, successfully concluded its two-day event on October 17 and 18, 2024, establishing new benchmarks in corporate culture and personal well-being. With over 40 international and national experts addressing mindfulness, emotional intelligence, and neuroscience, the summit highlighted how these principles are essential in transforming leadership, enhancing employee engagement, and fostering sustainable well-being within organizations. The evolving workplace landscape, particularly the increasing role of AI, requires a renewed focus on human-centric leadership and emotional resilience. The summit provided a platform for forward-thinking leaders to explore how mindfulness can effectively bridge this gap, ensuring both corporate excellence and employee well-being . Behl, a global mindfulness expert and founder of the Mindful Science Centre, shared, "With this book, I want to demystify mindfulness and make it accessible to everyone. Mindfulness is not a complex or distant concept, but a practical tool for reducing stress, improving focus, and fostering deeper connections in both personal and professional settings." The Mindfulness India Summit 2024 has successfully proven that mindfulness is no longer a luxury but a necessity in modern corporate structures. By adopting mindfulness practices, organizations are not only creating more compassionate work environments but are also enhancing their overall performance and sustainability in a world increasingly shaped by technological and emotional complexity. The 2 days also saw the launch of Mindfulness Impact Awards, to honor organizations and individuals who have integrated mindfulness into their corporate structures and personal lives. These awards reflect the growing recognition that workplace culture directly affects employee productivity, creativity, and overall well-being. items.title: "No shortage of oil in world and prices should hopefully come down", says Hardeep Singh Puri
paras: Join our Whatsapp channel New Delhi [India], October 22 (ANI): Hardeep Singh Puri, Minister for Petroleum and Natural Gas on Tuesday said that there is no shortage of oil in the world and prices will come down soon, answering the question of the recent upswing in crude oil prices. Speaking to the media, the Union Minister cited global factors such as the war in the Middle East and voluntary cuts in oil production which are influencing the oil prices in the global market. He said, "It depends on global factors. One thing is very clear, there is no shortage of oil in the world...Today, more and more oil is coming on the market...There are other factors like geopolitical tensions. So, there is no shortage of oil but if there is tension in one part of the world, then the freight cost, and insurance freight cost will go up. Today, let us all hope that better sense prevails, that call for peace that our Prime Minister has been making from every forum...There is more than enough oil in the world and prices should hopefully come down. That's my expectation..." "If there's tension in one part of the world, then the cost of, if you have to take a longer route, then the cost of the freight cost, the insurance rate cost, that will go up...There's more than enough oil in the world, and prices should hopefully come down," he commented in his personal capacity.

The union minister said many countries such as Brazil, and Guayana among others are coming with their oil. Citing the stable prices in the last 3 years, the minister said that the government is taking every possible step to ensure stable oil prices. "Central government at every stage has stepped in to cushion and bring the prices down from November 2021 to May 2022. Now there are some global factors. The cost at the retail point is determined by the cost of the barrel in the international market plus the cost of transportation, freight, insurance, retailers, refining cost and margin, then dealers, margin, etc. We are solving all the problems we can, now you tell the global community to hold and bring them down," he added. This comes after oil prices rose nearly 2 per cent on Monday, reclaiming major losses from last week's sell-off. Brent crude features upped by $1.44, or 1.97 per cent in the afternoon. Earlier this month, Puri had said that the country is well-prepared to meet its growing energy demands, with a diverse range of oil sources. Speaking on the availability of oil in the global market, Puri emphasised that India has expanded its procurement base, moving from 27 suppliers to 39. (ANI)

items.title: Mukka Proteins Limited Announces Rs 98 Crore Preferential Issue for Acquisition and Expansion
paras: Join our Whatsapp channel VMPL Mumbai (Maharashtra) [India], October 22: Mukka Proteins Limited , India's largest fish meal and insect meal producer and a leader in the animal protein industry , has announced the approval of a preferential issue worth Rs 98 crore by its Board of Directors. This strategic move will help Mukka Proteins in its ongoing domestic and international acquisition and expansion efforts, reinforcing its position in the global market. A significant portion of the funding will come from the promoter and promoter group, underlining their commitment to the company's robust growth strategy. The preferential issue will comprise up to 1.96 crore equity shares at Rs50 per share, aggregating to Rs98 crore. This price includes a premium of Rs49 per share on the face value of Rs1. Mukka Proteins will use the raised capital to enhance production capabilities and meet the growing global demand for sustainable and high-quality protein solutions, particularly in the fishmeal and insect meal sectors. In a clear show of confidence, Mukka Proteins' promoters have committed to a capital infusion of INR 60 crore through a preferential allotment of equity shares. This significant financial backing will be used to strengthen the company's financial position, reduce debt, and fund key operational improvements. Mukka Proteins has consistently embraced sustainability, having commercialized insect protein as a significant innovation for the aquaculture and animal feed industry. The company's waste-to-food initiatives have contributed to environmental sustainability, particularly in collaboration with the Mangaluru municipality for waste management. These efforts not only align with global environmental best practices but also enhance circular economy processes, focusing on converting municipal waste into valuable protein and oil products. Mukka Proteins is known for its strong commitment to ecological preservation, evident through the development of sustainable products such as fishmeal, fish oil, and insect protein. As a key player in the aquaculture and nutraceutical markets, Mukka contributes 25-30% of the market share in India's fishmeal and fish oil industry. The company plans to expand its operations further, capitalizing on this capital infusion to enter new markets and enhance its global footprint.

This issuance is subject to necessary statutory and regulatory approvals, including shareholder approval at the upcoming Extra-Ordinary General Meeting (EGM) on November 16, 2024. Managing Director and CEO Harris commented, "This preferential issue is a major milestone for Mukka Proteins as we continue to strengthen our market position. Our growth plans remain firmly rooted in sustainability, and this capital will enable us to scale up production, diversify our product offerings, and reinforce our commitment to responsible and eco-friendly business practices." Mukka Proteins Limited is poised to capture new opportunities in the animal protein sector, reinforcing its legacy of innovation, sustainability, and operational excellence. Mukka Proteins Limited : Mukka Proteins Limited is a leading manufacturer and exporter of fish meal , fish oil, and other protein products. The company has built a reputation for delivering high-quality, sustainable protein products to a global customer base. With a commitment to innovation and quality, Mukka Proteins serves industries including aquaculture, pet food, and agriculture across multiple continents. Headquartered in Mangalore, India, Mukka Proteins operates state-of-the-art processing facilities that meet stringent international standards. The company is dedicated to sustainable practices and has been at the forefront of environmental stewardship within the protein processing industry. items.title: Hon’ble Prime Minister of India inaugurates the Reserve Bank of India’s Data Centre and Cybersecurity Training Institute
paras: The Hon’ble Prime Minister of India, Shri Narendra Modi, today inaugurated the Reserve Bank of India’s newly established Data Centre and Cybersecurity Training Institute in Bhubaneswar, Odisha. This marks a significant milestone in strengthening the technological foundation of India’s financial system. Hon’ble Governor of Odisha, Shri Brajmohan Ram, Hon’ble Chief Minister of Odisha, Shri Mohan Charan Majhi; Hon’ble Union Finance and Corporate Affairs Minister, Smt. Nirmala Sitharaman; Hon’ble Union Minister for Tribal Affairs, Shri Jual Oram; Hon’ble Deputy Chief Ministers of Odisha, Shri Kanak Vardhan Singh Deo and Smt. Pravati Parida, and Hon’ble Members of Parliament, Shri Manmohan Samal and Smt. Aparajita Sarangi, also graced the event. 2. In his address, the Hon’ble Prime Minister highlighted the significance of the institutions inaugurated today - the Data Centre and the Cybersecurity Training Institute - in strengthening India’s digital financial infrastructure and advancing its technological self-reliance. The PM described the facility as a reflection of India’s changing approach to governance focused on taking the benefits of economic development to every region and every citizen. He emphasised that a secure banking system needs secure digital infrastructure supported by robust data centres and powerful computing systems and RBI’s new Data Centre is a critical step in this direction. 3. In her address, the Hon’ble Union Minister of Finance and Corporate Affairs underscored the strategic importance of resilient infrastructure in safeguarding financial stability and supporting sustained economic growth. She further said that the new Data Centre will house RBI’s mission-critical systems, including RTGS and NEFT, while the Training Institute will build expertise in cybersecurity, AI and other emerging technologies. 4.
